# {.inverse}

::: {.r-fit-text}
Handwriting practice
<br>for a six-year-old
:::

::: {.notes}
COLD OPEN. No thesis, no framing, no agenda slide. Just the story.

"My daughter is learning to write. I wanted trace-the-sentence practice sheets.
So I asked an agent to make me one."

Do not say the word Quarto yet.
:::

## What I asked for

> Make me a one-page handwriting practice sheet.
> Dotted trace lines, three sentences, big friendly type.

::: {.notes}
Read it out loud. It's a completely reasonable prompt. Everyone in the room has
written a prompt like this.
:::

## What I got

::: {.leftcol}
It looked great.

Three sentences. Big friendly type. Dotted lines.

[One of the sentences wasn't the one I asked for.]{.red}
:::

::: {.rightcol}
> **[SCREENSHOT — directly-generated sheet, the drifted sentence circled]**
:::

::: {.notes}
Land it lightly, not as a gotcha. The format was perfect. The *content* drifted.

Key beat: I didn't notice at first. My daughter did — she read it out loud.
:::

## So I asked it to fix that one sentence

::: {.leftcol}
And it regenerated the whole sheet.

New spacing. Different line weights. A *different* third sentence.
:::

::: {.rightcol}
> **[SCREENSHOT — the "fixed" sheet, now different in other ways]**
:::

::: {.notes}
This is the real problem, and it's not "LLMs make mistakes." It's that there was
no way to make a small change. Every edit is a full regeneration.
:::

## {.inverse}

::: {.r-fit-text}
Where *is*
<br>the sentence?
:::

::: {.notes}
Slow down here. This is the question the whole talk answers.

In that PDF, there is no line of anything that IS that sentence. It's smeared
across one probabilistic pass. Point at it — you can't.
:::

## {.inverse}

::: {.r-fit-text}
You already believe
<br>everything I'm about to say.
:::

[I want to know why almost none of us do it.]{.font140 .orange}

::: {.notes}
THE DEFUSING LINE. Say the audience's objection out loud before they can think it.

"This is a room full of people who believe in reproducibility. And I'd bet most
of us, when we open a chat window, ask for the finished thing anyway."

This converts their prior knowledge from a liability into complicity.
:::

# Entanglement {.inverse}

## The content has no address

::: {.leftcol}
When an agent generates a finished document, content and structure come out
**woven together** in a single probabilistic pass.

Nothing in it has a location.

To change one sentence, you regenerate everything — and hope.
:::

::: {.rightcol}
[There is no file, no line, no cell that *is* that sentence.]{.font120}
:::

::: {.notes}
Define entanglement operationally, not metaphorically. "The content has no
address" is the sticky version.

Give them the test they can apply to their own work: can you point at it?
:::

## When does it weave?

> **[FIGURE — "when does it weave?" diagram]**
> Two stacked rows, identical output at the end of each.
> Row 1: Me → agent ⇒ document (woven here, probabilistically).
> Row 2: Me → agent → `.qmd` + data → render → same document
> (woven here, deterministically), plus green edit arrows from Me.
> 3 clicks. Source: `images/entanglement-diagram/`

::: {.notes}
Both approaches weave content and format together. The only question is WHEN —
and by what.

The output is identical in both rows. That's the point. The difference isn't
what comes out, it's whether you can reach in before it does.

Optional one-liner for this room: "weave" isn't my metaphor. It's literate
programming's own word — Sweave, then knitr. Quarto has always been a weaving
tool. I'm just arguing we should weave later.
:::

## Give the content an address

::: {.leftcol}
```r
# sentences.csv
sentence
"The quick brown fox jumps."
"A red kite flew over the hill."
"We read books on rainy days."
```

The `.qmd` is structure. The CSV is content.

Changing a sentence is **editing row 3 of a text file.**
:::

::: {.rightcol}
> **[PDF — same sheet, rendered from the CSV]**
:::

::: {.notes}
Same sheet. But now the sentence has an address, and I can change it without
asking anyone's permission — including the model's.

The agent wrote the .qmd. It never touched the sentences.
:::

## But your prose doesn't go in a CSV

::: {.leftcol}
[**Prose** stays in the `.qmd`.]{.blue}

Its address is a **line number**. The agent's edit arrives as a diff you can
read in ten seconds.
:::

::: {.rightcol}
[**Values that must be exact** live in data + code.]{.amber}

Not just locatable — **recomputed.** Never typed by anyone.
:::

[The move isn't "extract everything."]{.font120}
[It's "stop asking for the artifact."]{.font120 .green}

::: {.notes}
NAME THE OBJECTION FIRST. Someone is already thinking "I'm not putting my
paragraphs in a spreadsheet." They're right, and say so.

The handwriting sheet is a case where the content genuinely IS data — a list of
items to typeset. Don't over-generalize from it.

Two tiers, and both are things a fused artifact denies you: prose gets
*located*, data gets *derived*.
:::

## {.inverse}

::: {.r-fit-text}
Agents should write the source,
<br>not the artifact.
:::

::: {.notes}
SPINE SENTENCE, 1 of 3. Let it sit. This is the whole talk in seven words.

Note what it does NOT say: "put your content in data files." It says hand me the
source. Everything else follows from that.
:::

## You can't prompt your way to correctness

[You architect it.]{.font160 .blue}

::: {.notes}
The prescription. Note what it's NOT: better prompts, better evals, better
models. Shrink the surface that has to be probabilistic at all.
:::

# And then something I didn't expect {.inverse}

::: {.notes}
ACT 3. THE TURN. The audience is braced for a worthiness argument about
correctness. Give them an argument about cost instead.
:::

## It's also cheaper

Same prompt, same model. Only the output target changes.

| Asked for | Direct | Via `.qmd` |
|-----------|-------:|-----------:|
| Word      | 8,097  | **1,121**  |
| HTML      | 4,046  | **1,022**  |
| PDF       | 1,992  | **1,123**  |
| Markdown  | 1,267  | **1,282**  |

::: {.notes}
Don't read the numbers. Point at the SHAPE.

Left column: wild swings — 1,267 up to 8,097 — because the agent is typing the
artifact, and some artifacts are miserable to type. Office Open XML is 8,000
tokens of raw XML.

Right column is FLAT. Around a thousand, every time. The agent never spends a
token on the artifact — the renderer does that part for free.

Note the honest row: for Markdown it's a wash. Say so. Costs nothing, buys trust.
:::

## And that's just the first turn

> **[CHART or TABLE — multi-turn token cost]**
> Cost growth across an agentic session, direct output vs. `.qmd`.
> Author to supply — numbers from the revised blog post.

Every edit to a fused artifact **regenerates the whole thing.**

An edit to a `.qmd` is a **diff.**

::: {.notes}
CALLBACK TO ACT 1 — make it explicit: "remember the sheet? I asked it to change
one sentence and it rebuilt the entire page. That wasn't just a correctness
problem. I paid full price for it."

This is the same phenomenon as the cold open, now measured instead of narrated.
The single-shot table understates the case, because nobody generates once —
you iterate. The gap doesn't stay at 7×; it compounds with every turn.
:::

## {.inverse}

::: {.r-fit-text}
Reproducibility used to be a tax.
:::

[Now it's the discount.]{.font160 .green}

::: {.notes}
THE TURN, stated. This is the most quotable moment in the talk — earn the pause.

For fifteen years, doing this right cost you something up front. Everyone in
this room believes in it, and everyone in this room has a folder of scripts they
never turned into a .qmd, because the tax was real.

The tax is gone. The virtuous path is now the lazy path.
:::

# This is how you build anything {.inverse}

::: {.notes}
ACT 4. THE DASHBOARD. 6 minutes. This is the most concrete material in the talk
and it is deliberately in the middle, where running long can't reach it.
:::

## A multi-page data product

> **[RECORDING — silent screen capture, ~75s]**
> Multi-page Quarto site: JS plotting libraries, Shinylive, React components.

::: {.notes}
No audio. Let it play and narrate lightly. Don't tour features — this is
evidence, not a demo.

Use the phrase "data product." It's this session's shared vocabulary.
:::

## Same move, bigger artifact

::: {.leftcol}
[**The agent wrote:**]{.blue}

- page structure and layout
- the YAML
- chunk logic
- the embedding glue
:::

::: {.rightcol}
[**The agent never touched:**]{.amber}

- the data
- the numbers
- the labels anyone reads
:::

[Every number on every page is computed at render time.]{.font120}

::: {.notes}
This is the modularity claim, made concrete instead of asserted.

The scale changed. The move didn't. A one-page PDF for a six-year-old and a
multi-page dashboard are the same architecture.
:::

::: {.r-fit-text}
Agents should write the source,

# "So why not just ask for HTML?" {.inverse}

::: {.notes}
ACT 5. Name the objection before the audience can. Do NOT reference anyone
else's post — this is your objection, in your voice.
:::

## Honestly — the case for HTML is good

- Rich, structured, immediately viewable
- No toolchain, no render step, opens anywhere
- Infinitely more useful than a wall of Markdown
- Agents are *very* good at it

[If it's single-use and disposable, take the HTML.]{.gray}

::: {.notes}
Make this case generously and at full strength. Steelman it. You lose nothing by
being fair here and you gain the room's trust for the turn.

The throwaway-editor concession is genuine — say it and mean it.
:::

## Not a screenshot

> **[INLINE CHART — live interactive plot rendered into this slide]**

::: {.notes}
Quarto gives you all of it. This is rendered and interactive, right here, in the
slide you're looking at.
:::

## {.inverse}

::: {.r-fit-text}
This deck is
<br>a `.qmd` file.
:::

::: {.notes}
The meta-reveal. Proof by existence — and the closest thing to a live demo this
talk is allowed to have. Let it land.
:::

## But HTML can't tell you it's broken

::: {.leftcol}
[**HTML**]{.red}

No compile step.

Malformed output still renders as *something*.

The agent cannot tell whether it succeeded.
:::

::: {.rightcol}
[**`.qmd`**]{.blue}

Bad cross-reference, failed chunk, invalid YAML → **loud, deterministic error.**

The agent reads it and fixes it — without you.
:::

::: {.notes}
THE KILL SHOT of Act 5. This is the sharpest thing in the talk.

Documents just got a compile step. Code has had one for decades. Documents get
one exactly at the moment their authors became probabilistic.
:::

## Checkable twice

::: {.leftcol}
[**By machine**]{.darkgreen}

`quarto render` is a compile step. Failures are loud and specific.
:::

::: {.rightcol}
[**By human**]{.darkgreen}

Plain text means the agent's edit is a **diff**. Review scales with the change,
not the document.
:::

[A `.docx` "diff" is noise. A three-line `.qmd` diff is a review.]{.font120}

::: {.notes}
Both halves matter. git revert is a one-command undo for any agent mistake.
:::

## One honest caveat

Render passing ≠ analysis correct.

It's the same guarantee compilation gives code — **no more, no less.**

::: {.notes}
State the limit plainly. It costs 10 seconds and buys more credibility than any
other slide in the deck.
:::

# Close {.inverse}

## You don't need to know Quarto

Change **one word** in your prompt.

[Ask for the `.qmd`.]{.font160 .blue}

::: {.notes}
The accessibility close. This is for everyone in the room, not just power users.
:::

## Make this work Monday

1. Put *"always run `quarto render` before finishing"* in your `CLAUDE.md`
2. Have the agent work on a branch, so edits arrive as diffs
3. Keep data in files the `.qmd` reads — never in the prompt

::: {.notes}
Photographable. Three lines. This is the whole practicum, and it converts
inspiration into action without costing narrative time.

Deeper material (Quarto skills, Lua filters, parameterized reports) is a "come
find me after" line.
:::
